▪ 7- and 10-year: inside their covering ranges, the 10-year ~1bp from finishing
▪ 2- and 5-year: shorts still on

The surge in AI imports pushed the US goods trade deficit to $134.9B in September (est. $130.2B), the widest since March 2025 and a third straight monthly increase, per the Census Bureau’s advance report.

▪️ Still exports grew +2.6% to $209.2B, the third highest on record
▪️ Imports (which are  +2.4% to $344.1B a fresh record
▪️ Capital goods imports, which include computers, chips and telecom gear,  +7.5% to a record $157.4B, up 77% from a year ago
▪️ Consumer goods imports +3.1%, the most in four months, but still down 12% from a year ago
▪️ Industrial supplies imports (incl. oil and gold) -6.0% after jumping 17.1% in August

Goldman noted: "The capital goods category has been a primary contributor to the widening trade deficit this year and has partially offset the impact of rapidly rising AI business investment on GDP growth."

Before today’s data, the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow had net exports subtracting 2.86 points from Q3 GDP. The full trade balance report, with services, is out November 4.

Goldman: Tightening cycles have historically been longer and larger than this one is expected to be, and there are a limited number of historical examples of modest hiking cycles. 

1997 and 2015 were cycles where the Fed hiked only once, and 1999 was the next smallest hiking cycle at 175bps of tightening. We bucket those three smallest and shortest hiking cycles (1997, 1999, and 2015) as “modest” tightening cycles and the larger and longer cycles as “other cycles” (1983, 1988, 1994, 2004, 2016, 2022). 

The exhibits  show median asset performance across those categories and across the full sample in the one year before and the two years following the first Fed hike, indexed to the day of the hike, for the S&P 500, the 2-year Treasury yield, the slope of the yield curve (10y minus 2y yields), and the real trade-weighted US Dollar.

-Equities tend to struggle after the first hike but recover quickly. 

-Both front- and long-end yields tend to rise in anticipation of the first hike. In the median, yields tend to peak locally shortly after the first hike in modest hiking cycles but continue to rise for some time in other cycles.

-The curve tends to flatten into the first hike, and this flattening tends to continue after the first hike...Our rates strategists similarly noted that front-end forward yields usually peak around the end of rate hikes and after the peak in inflation is confirmed in the data and that, after the peak in forward yields, flattening tends to stop as the curve rallies in parallel.

-The real trade-weighted US Dollar tends to strengthen into the first hike, but its performance afterwards has been mixed across cycles.

Of the major banks, the only one I know that as of this week was still calling for a rate hike today was BofA although it's a curious call given they have "low conviction":

Aditya Bhave and team are sticking with their out-of-consensus call saying the large beat in September inflation “bolsters the case for an Oct hike,” but concedes it would be “a heavy lift,” with markets pricing only about a 10% chance and the meeting falling six days before the midterm elections. Despite its “strong conviction that the Fed should hike,” BofA says it has “only low conviction that it will,” makng the reasoning behind sticking with the call a little questionable.

BofA frames the meeting as a test of Chair Kevin Warsh’s resolve to bring a “sea change” to the Fed’s forward guidance. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams gave what BofA calls “heavy-handed forward guidance” that led markets to price out an October hike. 

Whichever way the Fed goes, BofA says Warsh’s job at the press conference will be to head off a “policy error” trade. A hike risks markets pricing in over-tightening, which BofA says could bring a large correction in risk assets and a flatter yield curve. 

A hold invites questions about the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility. It also risks a repeat of the July press conference: a steeper curve, a weaker dollar and a moderate selloff in risk assets.

A chart in the @dailychartbook nightly email caught my eye from Goldman's Tony Pasquariello: "The markets have suddenly engaged in an intense debate around both the availability AND the cost of capital. Our AI leaders-vs-laggards basket was up nearly 100% YTD at the end of June; in the time since, the entirety of that performance has been given back."

As he intimates the timing lines up pretty good with the headlines surrounding the shift to debt-funded AI capex: 
1 - Mid-June, Goldman flagged consensus hyperscaler capex of $770B this year, roughly 100% of operating cash flow (vs. a ~40% 10-yr avg), and Nvidia launched a $20B bond sale, its first since 2021 
2 - Incremental debt had gone from 9% of hyperscaler capex in FY2024 to 32% over the last twelve months 
3 - AI-related issuers now pay ~115 bp over Treasuries vs. 78 bp for the broader IG market, and Goldman sees $420B of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, up 60%

Worth remembering though this is a spread. "Gave back 100%" means the gap reclosed, not that AI stocks necessarily round-tripped, but there's no question that the market got a wake-up call at the peak that all this AI spending wasn't coming out of the hyperscalers' pockets.

The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index jumps 7.5 points in October to 91.7, the highest since June and far above the 81.0 expected. It was the biggest beat since May 2025 per ZeroHedge, and the first increase in four months per Bloomberg.

▪ All five components improved
▪ Present Situation: 120.4, a six-month high per Bloomberg. Net business conditions turned positive again at +3.6%, from −1.2%
▪ Labor differential: Jobs “plentiful”: 26.7%, a six-month high. “Hard to get” unchanged at 21.4%
▪ Expectations: 72.6, “only partially reversing three consecutive monthly declines,” and still below the 80 level the Conference Board has linked to recession
▪ Expected jobs still negative at −11.1%, but expected income rose to +6.7%
▪ Average 12-month inflation expectations: 5.8%, which “remained elevated”
▪ 49.6% expect higher stock prices, against a 35.7% long-run average (Yardeni Research)
▪ Spending plans weakened: durable goods “dropped across the board,” and services were “generally lower” except movies, live entertainment and sports
▪ Gains were narrow: on a six-month basis, only under-35s and households earning $100,000+ saw confidence rise. Confidence improved “much more so for Republicans”

The Conference Board’s McCormick: the rebound “was in line with retail gasoline prices easing,” but confidence “remained on the long-term downward trend.”

Israelis are voting today in what many on both sides call the most consequential election in the country’s history. It’s the first since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that followed, and turnout is running at the fastest pace in nearly half a century, per Reuters.

The choice is stark. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is running on his record against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, backed by an endorsement from President Trump, and says only he can keep the country safe. His main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is campaigning on accountability for Oct. 7, per the FT. That includes a state inquiry that Netanyahu’s coalition has resisted, reversing parts of the judicial overhaul and ending the military-service exemption for ultra-Orthodox men. On security, though, the gap is narrower. Both oppose a Palestinian state, and Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza within 18 months, per the WSJ.

What the vote probably won’t deliver quickly is a government. Final polls had Eisenkot’s bloc at about 54 seats and Netanyahu’s coalition at about 50, both short of the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, with Arab and unaligned parties holding the rest, per the FT. Both camps have pledged not to rely on the Arab parties. The final count is expected by Friday, with official results on Nov. 4. President Isaac Herzog will then designate a candidate, who gets up to 42 days to build a coalition, per Al Jazeera. If that fails, the process can pass to another candidate and then to parliament before new elections are called. That sequence produced four inconclusive elections between 2019 and 2021. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister throughout, leaving him free to act on his pledge to resume the war with Iran, Bloomberg notes. Herzog has said he’ll try to avoid a repeat, raising the prospect that he pushes for a national unity government, per the FT.

Prediction markets lean toward change: Polymarket bettors gave Eisenkot about a 60% chance of becoming prime minister and Netanyahu 27%. As Brazil showed on Sunday, though, they can be quite wrong.

President Isaac Herzog will then designate a candidate, who gets up to 42 days to build a coalition, per Al Jazeera. If that fails, the process can pass to another candidate and then to parliament before new elections are called. That sequence produced four inconclusive elections between 2019 and 2021. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister throughout, leaving him free to act on his pledge to resume the war with Iran, Bloomberg notes. Herzog has said he’ll try to avoid a repeat, raising the prospect that he pushes for a national unity government, per the FT.

Prediction markets lean toward change: Polymarket bettors gave Eisenkot about a 60% chance of becoming prime minister and Netanyahu 27%. As Brazil showed on Sunday, though, they can be quite wrong.
